title: Modern Physics
lines: Modern physics questions are usually short and factual, with simple arithmetic in electronvolts or powers of ten. Learn the key experiments, what each one proved, and the conservation rules for nuclear equations. Use h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
## Photons and photon energy
- Light energy comes in packets called photons. Energy of one photon: E = hf = hc/λ. Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) means more energetic photons.
- Handy shortcut: hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, so E(in eV) ≈ 1240/λ(in nm). Red light (about 620 nm) has photons of about 2 eV; violet (about 400 nm) about 3.1 eV.
- The brightness (intensity) of light depends on how many photons arrive per second, not on the energy of each.
> Example: Find the energy of a photon of wavelength 6.6 × 10⁻⁷ m, in joules and in eV.
## The photoelectric effect
- Light shining on a metal can eject electrons. Each electron absorbs exactly one photon.
- Einstein's equation: E(k,max) = hf − W₀, where W₀ is the work function of the metal (the minimum energy to free an electron).
- Threshold frequency f₀ = W₀/h. Below f₀ no electrons come out, however bright the light. Above f₀ electrons are emitted almost instantly, even with dim light.
- Brighter light (same frequency) releases more electrons per second (larger saturation current), but does not raise their maximum kinetic energy.
- Stopping voltage U(c): the reverse voltage that just stops the fastest electrons, eU(c) = E(k,max).
- Graph of E(k,max) against f: a straight line with gradient h, crossing the f-axis at f₀. Every metal gives a line with the same gradient.
> Example: Photons of 4.0 eV fall on a metal with work function 2.3 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons and the stopping voltage.
! Trap: doubling the intensity doubles the photocurrent but leaves the stopping voltage unchanged. Only the frequency changes the stopping voltage.
## Wave-particle duality
- Light shows wave behaviour (interference, diffraction) and particle behaviour (photoelectric effect, Compton scattering). Neither picture alone explains everything.
- Matter also has a wave nature: a particle of momentum p has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p. Electron diffraction by crystals confirmed it.
- Photon momentum: p = h/λ.
- Everyday objects have huge momenta, so their wavelengths are far too small to notice.
> Example: An electron has momentum 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s. Find its de Broglie wavelength.
> λ = h/p = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why electrons diffract.
! Trap: a faster electron has a shorter de Broglie wavelength, not a longer one.
## The Bohr model and energy levels
- Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment (most alphas pass straight through gold foil, a very few bounce back) showed that an atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
- Bohr's model of hydrogen: the electron can only occupy certain orbits with fixed energies, E(n) = −13.6/n² eV (n = 1, 2, 3 ...). n = 1 is the ground state. Orbit radius r(n) = n²r₁.

- An electron moving from a higher level m to a lower level n emits a photon with hf = E(m) − E(n). Absorbing a photon raises it, but only if the photon's energy exactly matches a gap (or exceeds the ionisation energy).
- Ionisation energy from the ground state is 13.6 eV.
- A collection of atoms in level n can emit n(n − 1)/2 different photon energies as they fall back to the ground state.
- In a higher orbit the electron's kinetic energy is smaller, its potential energy larger, and the total energy larger (less negative).
> Example: Find the photon energy when a hydrogen electron falls from n = 2 to n = 1, and from n = 3 to n = 2.
> E(2) = −3.4 eV, E(1) = −13.6 eV: photon 10.2 eV (ultraviolet). E(3) = −1.51 eV: 3 → 2 gives 3.4 − 1.51 = 1.89 eV (red visible light).
> Example: How many different spectral lines can hydrogen atoms in the n = 4 level emit?
! Trap: a 12 eV photon is not absorbed by ground-state hydrogen, because no gap equals 12 eV. A 12 eV electron, however, can give 10.2 eV to the atom and keep the rest.
## Spectra
- A continuous spectrum (all colours) comes from hot solids and dense hot gases.
- A line emission spectrum (bright lines) comes from hot thin gases. An absorption spectrum (dark lines on a continuous background) appears when white light passes through a cooler gas.
- The lines are at the same wavelengths for emission and absorption of a given element, so spectra identify elements, for example in the Sun and stars.
## Nuclear structure
- A nucleus contains Z protons and N neutrons; the mass number A = Z + N. Notation: element symbol with A at top left and Z at bottom left, written here as ²³⁸₉₂U.
- Isotopes have the same Z (same element, same chemistry) but different N.
- The strong nuclear force holds nucleons together. It is very strong but acts only over about 10⁻¹⁵ m.
## Radioactivity
- Alpha (α): a helium nucleus ⁴₂He, charge +2e. Strongly ionising, stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air. Alpha decay: A decreases by 4, Z by 2.
- Beta (β): a fast electron created when a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton. Stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Beta decay: A unchanged, Z increases by 1.
- Gamma (γ): high-energy electromagnetic radiation, emitted after α or β decay as the nucleus settles. Weakly ionising, very penetrating (thick lead or concrete). A and Z unchanged.
- In electric or magnetic fields α and β bend in opposite directions; γ is not deflected.
> Example: ²³⁸₉₂U decays to ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb. How many α and β decays occur?
> A falls by 32, so there are 32/4 = 8 alpha decays, which lower Z by 16. Z actually falls by 10, so 6 beta decays raised it by 6.
! Trick: count alphas first from the mass number (only alphas change A), then fix Z with betas.
## Half-life
- Half-life T: the time for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. Remaining amount N = N₀(½)^(t/T).
- Half-life is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination. It is a statistical rule for large numbers of nuclei; for a few nuclei it predicts nothing.
> Example: A sample contains 16 g of an isotope with half-life 5 days. How much is left after 15 days?
> 15 days is 3 half-lives: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 g.
! Trap: after two half-lives, one quarter remains, not zero. Three quarters have decayed.
## Nuclear equations
- In every nuclear reaction both the mass number (sum of top numbers) and the charge number (sum of bottom numbers) are conserved.
- Useful particles: proton ¹₁H, neutron ¹₀n, electron ⁰₋₁e, alpha ⁴₂He.
> Example: Balance ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + X. Identify X.
> Top: 14 + 4 = 17 + A, so A = 1. Bottom: 7 + 2 = 8 + Z, so Z = 1. X is a proton, ¹₁H (the reaction in which Rutherford found the proton).
! Trap: mass number is conserved but mass is not. A small mass defect becomes released energy.
## Mass-energy, fission and fusion
- E = mc²; energy released in a reaction ΔE = Δm c². In atomic units, 1 u corresponds to about 931.5 MeV.

- Binding energy is the energy needed to split a nucleus into separate nucleons. Binding energy per nucleon is largest for medium nuclei near iron, so splitting heavy nuclei (fission) and joining light nuclei (fusion) both release energy.

- Fission: a slow neutron splits uranium-235, for example ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n. The released neutrons can cause a chain reaction if the mass exceeds the critical mass. In a reactor, control rods absorb neutrons and a moderator slows them.
- Fusion: for example ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n. It needs extremely high temperatures to overcome the repulsion between nuclei. It powers the Sun and gives more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission.
> Example: A reaction has a mass defect of 1 × 10⁻³⁰ kg. Find the energy released.
> Example: Check the fission equation above.
## Exam checklist
- Photoelectric: frequency decides energy, intensity decides number.
- Energy levels: photon energy must equal a gap exactly.
- Nuclear equations: balance A and Z; count alphas first.
